paragraphs.text: This psalm is by the Jews called Hillel gadol, the great gratulatory. See Psa 106:1; Psa 107:1; Psa 118:1.
paragraphs.anchor: O give thanks unto the Lord

paragraphs.text: His covenant mercy, that precious Church privilege; this is perpetual to his people, and should perpetually shine as a picture in our hearts. For which purpose this psalm was appointed to be daily sung in the old church, by the Levites, 1Ch 16:41.
paragraphs.anchor: For his mercy endureth for ever

paragraphs.text: This is the foot or burden of the whole song; neither is it any idle repetition, but a notable expression of the saints’ unsatisfiableness in praising God for his never failing mercy. These heavenly birds, having got a note, record it over and over. In the last psalm there are but six verses, yet twelve Hallelujahs.
paragraphs.anchor: For his mercy endureth for ever

paragraphs.text: That is, to God the Son, saith Jerome; as by God of gods, saith he, in the former verse, is meant God the Father; who, because they are no more but one God only, it is added,
paragraphs.anchor: O give thanks unto the Lord of lords

paragraphs.text: Wondrous things the creature may do, but not wonders; mira sed non miracula. God alone is the great Thaumaturgus, that is, wonder worker.
paragraphs.anchor: To him who alone doeth great wonders

paragraphs.text: Singulari ingenio et summa industria, yet without tool or toil. See Heb 11:10. {See Trapp on "Heb 11:10"}
paragraphs.anchor: To him that by wisdom, &c.

paragraphs.text: A perpetual mercy to all earthly creatures, as is elsewhere set forth, Gen 1:9 Psa 24:2.
paragraphs.anchor: To him that stretched out the earth, &c.

paragraphs.text: Without which we should have no more comfort of the air we breathe in than the Egyptians had in that three days’ darkness. Now the sun and moon are called great luminaries, not great stars or bodies (for the sun is less than some stars, and the moon is least of all), first, for the excellence of light which these two do more abundantly impart to the earth; and, secondly, for the effects they work; the sun by his access making all green and flourishing, and the contrary by his recess; the moon by its various aspect causing humours and marrows to increase or decrease, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: To him that made great lights

paragraphs.text: Heb. for the rulings by day, sc. by his light, heat, motion, and influences, whereby he worketh upon these inferior bodies, being a servant to all, as his name importeth, notwithstanding his ruledom; and therefore in no wise to have been worshipped.
paragraphs.anchor: The sun to rule by day

paragraphs.text: For by day they all veil to the sun; from whom also they borrow much of their light. The moon hath her name in Hebrew from moisture, as refreshing the earth with her cool influences; and thrusting forth precious things therein, Deu 33:14.
paragraphs.anchor: The moon and stars to rule by night

paragraphs.text: See Psa 135:8.

paragraphs.text: viz. By that last plague; for the former would not do. God will have the better of his enemies, for the good of his people; for it is not fit that he should lay down the bucklers first.
paragraphs.anchor: And brought out Israel

paragraphs.anchor: And with a stretched out arm

paragraphs.text: Into twelve several parts, say the Jews, for the twelve tribes to pass through.
paragraphs.anchor: To him which divided the Red Sea

paragraphs.text: It is many times hail with the saints, when ill with the wicked. Abraham from the hill seeth Sodom on fire.
paragraphs.anchor: And made Israel to pass, &c.

paragraphs.text: Praecipitavit, pitched him in headlong; having before paved a way for him. Subito tollitur qui diu toleratur.
paragraphs.anchor: But overthrew Pharaoh

paragraphs.text: As a horse, that they should not stumble, Isa 63:13; as a shepherd his sheep; providing for them so, as never was any prince so served in his greatest pomp.
paragraphs.anchor: To him which led his people

paragraphs.text: Great, as those times accounted them, when every small city almost had their king; Canaan had thirty and more of them. Great also in regard of their stature and strength; for they were of the giant’s race, Deu 3:11-13 Amo 2:1

paragraphs.text: Still God helpeth those who are forsaken of their hopes, et vindictae gladium miserationis oleo emollit, as Nicephorus saith.
paragraphs.anchor: Who remembered us in our low estate

paragraphs.text: Or, broken us off, pulled us away, as by violence; for they would never else have loosed us. This is priori maior misericordia, a greater mercy than the former, saith Kimchi; to redeem is more than to preserve.
paragraphs.anchor: And hath redeemed us

paragraphs.text: Food agreeable to their several appetites and temperaments, suitable and seasonable.
paragraphs.anchor: Who giveth food to all flesh

paragraphs.text: His mercy in providing heaven for his people is more than all the rest.
